title: Mailing labels
prompt: The mailing house prints customers as surname, then initial: `Ines Okafor` becomes `Okafor, I.`. Write `solve(customers)` so it returns `customer_id` and `label`.
rules: The surname is the last word of `name` and the initial is the first letter of the first word, followed by a full stop: `Ana Maria Ruiz` gives `Ruiz, A.`. Letters keep the case they have.
Words are separated by one or more spaces; spaces at the start or end don't count.
A one-word name is printed as it is (`Cher` gives `Cher`). A missing name, or one made only of spaces, gives a missing label.
Return `customer_id` and `label`, both text, in that order. Keep every customer.
hints: This is easiest as a Python function: `words = name.split()`, then pick `words[-1]` and `words[0][0]`.
Handle the short cases before building the label: `None`, no words at all, and a single word.
Wrap it with `@F.udf("string")` and use it in `select` with `alias("label")`.
explanation: A UDF reads naturally here: return `None` for a missing name or one with no words, the word itself when there's only one, and otherwise `f"{words[-1]}, {words[0][0]}."`. `split()` without an argument ignores extra spaces; `split(" ")` keeps empty strings, so `words[0]` can be `""` and the job stops. Taking the second word as the surname breaks on three-word names, and returning an empty string for a blank name isn't the same as a missing label.
